newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss insurers urged to pay out Holocaust policies.
newsitem.headline: Swiss insurers urged to pay out Holocaust policies.

text.p: The U.S.-based civil rights group Simon Wiesenthal Centre called on Swiss insurers on Monday to honour unclaimed policies of Holocaust victims and survivors.

The group's leaders said one Swiss company, Winterthur Insurance Co, had already searched for unclaimed Jewish policies taken out in the years leading up to the Holocaust by Jewish victims and urged others to follow suit.
"There's never been a systematic effort to locate these individuals who were victims during World War Two or their heirs," its deputy dean Abraham Cooper told a news conference.

Several insurers in Germany, Italy and France are facing class-action suits filed by Holocaust survivors in the United States over charges that they refused to play claims on insurance policies of victims or their heirs.

The centre said Winterthur had paid out proceeds from three Jewish policies to the Nazis and turned over proceeds from another seven to a Swiss state agency under a government search in 1962 for unclaimed Holocaust assets.
But Winterthur, which first announced its Holocaust findings in January, said Wiesenthal researchers apparently misunderstood what they learned during a visit to its headquarters last week.
The three Jewish policies referred to were paid out to the owners or in one case to a widow, not to Nazis, it said, naming owners as Walter Goldstein, Benjamin Joseph and Dr S. Heilbronn.
"I can confirm that all three policies were paid out to the entitled private persons and not to the state (Nazi Germany)," Winterthur spokeswoman Anna-Marie Kappeler told Reuters.
Winterthur also said it paid out the dormant policies found in the 1960s search to a government-sponsored fund for Holocaust victims, not to a state agency.

Samuels said his centre had identified a list of 90 unclaimed policies bought at Winterthur in the years leading to the Holocaust, 20 of them on Jewish names. He claimed that most of the remainder were "probably" bought by Jews in Swiss names.
But Winterthur said its own research showed it held 34 policies from the war era whose owners had not been heard from in a decade or more.
Of these, 24 were Swiss domestic policies but the remaining ten may have belonged to victims of the Holocaust, based on the names, country of origin or date of the policies.
"We have shown the ten names to the Simon Wiesenthal Centre because we want to find the rightful owners or their heirs," the company spokeswoman said.
